item.title: Digga D Gets Three Months To Pay $268K In Drug Profits Or Face Prison
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Digga D was ordered to repay £201,039 within three months or face two years in prison, while his lawyer said he could pay.
item.content:encoded:
Digga D was given three months to repay $268,000, with two years in prison at stake if he failed to pay.

Judge Simon Hirst imposed the confiscation order at Lincoln Crown Court on October 21, the BBC reported.

The rapper, whose legal name is Rhys Herbert, had already been released from prison.

Judge Hirst had sentenced him to three years and 11 months on January 31, 2025. Digga D had pleaded guilty to drug import and supply charges.

The two sides had disagreed over how much he had sold and whether he did so for profit.

Digga D argued that much of the cannabis was for him and his circle, with only a small amount sold.

In those sentencing remarks, Judge Hirst rejected that account. He found that Digga D had sold at least 45 kilograms of cannabis for commercial profit. The judge also found that he had supplied the drug over at least seven months, from January through July 2023.

The financial order focused on the proceeds of the offenses. In its guidance, the Crown Prosecution Service explained that confiscation aimed to take away the financial benefit a defendant obtained through crime.

The amount a court seeks to recover can also depend on what the defendant can pay.

That calculation is not always the same as the total benefit figure. Courts generally start with the value of the criminal benefit, but a defendant can show that the assets available to meet the order are worth less. In that situation, the recoverable sum can be the smaller amount.

Nonpayment carries a separate enforcement process. The CPS guidance said authorities could ask the magistrates’ court to activate the prison term set in case of default. Serving that time would not wipe out the debt, so prison would not replace the obligation to pay the money.

The guidance also explained that unpaid confiscation sums can accrue interest after the payment deadline. Paying the full sum by the deadline avoids that interest and the risk of serving the default term.

At the October 21 hearing, defense lawyer Ryan Thompson told the court Digga D had the funds to pay, the BBC reported.

item.title: Chrisean Rock And Blueface’s Family Reunion Takes The Craziest Twist Ever
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: Blueface and Chrisean Rock's latest reconciliation appears to be unraveling after a frightening gun confrontation with the cops.
item.content:encoded:
Blueface may have finally reached his breaking point with Chrisean Rock. The pair had a frightening, terrifying confrontation involving armed cops. Their young son and a disagreement that has spilled into public view.

And just like that, the reconciliation that had everybody talking could be headed straight for the dumpster.

And just when we thought these two had finally found some peace! What happened?

The Cuh-RIP rapper and his equally wild partner are at odds following an October 19 incident in Santa Clarita, California, that resulted in Blueface being arrested. The whole ordeal began when authorities responded to a report of someone allegedly pointing a firearm at another person near a Yard House restaurant. This was another swatting situation that he’s been dealing with for a minute now.

Deputies arrived with guns drawn, only to discover there was apparently no armed suspect. A swatting hoax, y’all.

Blueface, per usual, still ended up in handcuffs.

Then his doting fiancee comes in the mix.

Chrisean Rock was there with their three-year-old son when the mess unfolded. And according to the couple’s subsequent statements, they have drastically different views of what happened.

Blueface was furious about Chrisean’s decision to retrieve their child from a vehicle while officers had their weapons drawn.

“I’m not a female I would never do that. I would never see a female in the middle of a motherf##king standoff and pick up my child.”

He took it to the next level in the rant.

“Man, killed this b#tch,” he said to the non-present police. “My son in the car…k#ll this b#tch. This b#tch 26 years old…k#ll this b#tch. My son is three years old. F#ck this b#tch. What the f#ck? You (women) really stand behind b#tches like “Yeah she’s loyal.” No, the b#tch is stupid. The b#tch is dumb.”

Wow. He emptied the clip. No pun intended.

Chrisean, however, insists she was protecting her family.

“They got the gun and put it towards Blue, b#tch! I went and got the baby from the car seat and walked out front of the front of the f#cking gun ni##a,” she yelled in a video.

She apparently believed standing beside Blueface during the terrifying encounter demonstrated loyalty.

“I’m sticking with you like a family, they had a gun in your face.”

Well, there you have it.

One person believes loyalty means standing together regardless of the circumstances. The other believes protecting their child should supersede everything, including romantic devotion.

Now, remember that these two recently appeared to be enjoying a romantic resurgence – engaged! We saw the proposal! The private jet photographs! And those happy family moments suggested their tumultuous history was over.

Not! Blueface – give it another shot! Get some therapy!

The saddest part is that their little boy was caught in the middle of an already dangerous situation.

Are Blueface and Chrisean Rock finally finished?

Or will another reconciliation follow once the emotions subside?

Let’s make peace over proving a point the big picture.

Maybe, we’ll get this again.

item.title: AKA Trial Witness Reports Threats As Others Ask To Stay Off TV
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: AKA trial witnesses asked to keep their faces off TV after the state said one witness received threats following his testimony.
item.content:encoded:
AKA‘s murder trial took a tense turn when the state said a witness had received threats after his face appeared in the news.

Prosecutor Elvis Gcweka raised the claim in the Durban High Court on October 20. He said the man told him about the threats after he took the stand the day before, EWN reported.

The news left other witnesses worried about being shown on TV. They still wanted to come to court and speak, Gcweka said. They asked to keep their faces off the screen because of fears for their safety or their work.

“Their only request is that their faces must not be shown on TV,” Gcweka said, The Citizen reported.

Judge Nomfundo Sipunzi then ruled that the next witness’s face must stay off TV. The order covered that witness, not every person yet to take the stand.

The reports did not name a sender or link the threats to any of the seven men on trial. The claim came from the state, not a court finding that one of the accused had threatened a witness.

The court had just heard about footage of AKA at the airport on the day he died. A man could be seen moving behind him, and the defense questioned who could be named from those images. The witness did not identify the man in the footage as one of the accused.

All seven men pleaded not guilty. The state must prove its case against each man, and the trial has not reached a verdict.

The new plea also came after a fight over what the public could see and hear from court. At first, Judge Sipunzi barred news reports on what witnesses said on the stand. She changed the rule on October 7, allowing the press to report their accounts and the exhibits shown in court.

But that change did not open the door to naming witnesses. Their names and personal details remained off limits under the court’s rule.

Last week, two witnesses spoke from another courtroom. They feared being named or facing the accused as they told the court about men they saw near the scene after the shots.

AKA and Tebello “Tibz” Motsoane were shot dead outside Wish restaurant in Durban on February 10, 2023.

item.title: Rick Ross Arraignment Delayed As Attorneys Say Charges Remain Unfiled
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Rick Ross' arraignment was delayed after his attorneys said prosecutors had not formally filed charges in his domestic violence case.
item.content:encoded:
Rick Ross‘ court date was pushed back Thursday. His lawyers said prosecutors had not yet filed formal charges in the case tied to claims of abuse by his ex-girlfriend, Jazzma Kendrick.

The rapper was due in a Miami court on October 22 for his arraignment, WSVN reported. His lawyers pointed to the lack of a formal filing. They did not say the case had been thrown out.

The case stems from Kendrick’s account of an August 28 attack. Ross, 50, whose legal name is William Leonard Roberts II, was arrested over claims of felony battery by strangulation and misdemeanor domestic violence.

He denied the claims when he got out of jail on October 1. Earlier that day, his lawyer, Bradley Horenstein, had entered a not-guilty plea for him, WSVN reported.

After leaving the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center, Ross spoke to reporters and said Kendrick had made up the claims against him.

Kendrick gave police a different account. She said the dispute began with an Instagram photo in which she was tagged. According to WSVN’s earlier report, she told police Ross thought she was seeing someone else and hit her when she denied it.

She also told police he struck her chest and pulled her by her ponytail. Kendrick shared photos of her injuries on social media and took her claims to police. Ross denied that account.

Police said their work went beyond her account. Miami Beach Police spokesperson Christopher Bess described what they had found, WSVN reported.

“[Detectives] also collected photographs of the injuries, surveillance video of the alleged incident, and they were able to establish probable cause for this arrest,” Bess said.

When Ross first went to court, Judge Mindy Glazer ordered him to stay away from the alleged victim and turn over any guns, AllHipHop previously reported. That October 1 report also listed October 22 as the date set for his arraignment.

His lawyer challenged the claims and asked the public to let the case play out. In a statement after Ross’ release, Horenstein also questioned why Kendrick went to police about a month after the alleged attack, WSVN reported.

item.title: Vic Mensa Calls Out Anti-Black Racism Without Backing Away From Palestine
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Vic Mensa challenged anti-Black racism in a new interview with Abdul El-Sayed while reaffirming his support for Palestine.
item.content:encoded:
Vic Mensa questioned why solidarity should require silence about anti-Black racism during his conversation with Abdul El-Sayed.

The rapper recalled children using a racial slur toward him in Palestine while reaffirming his support for Palestinian liberation.

El-Sayed, who is running for the U.S. Senate in Michigan, agreed.

“We need to address the elephant in the room,” he said.

Vic Mensa’s connection to the issue goes back years. In a January 2018 essay, he described traveling to Palestine the previous summer with Black artists, scholars and activists through Dream Defenders.

He drew parallels between the treatment he witnessed there and racial profiling in America.

Mensa made clear that his essay was not an attack on Jewish people. He framed it as criticism of the Israeli state’s treatment of Palestinian civilians, drawing on what he said he had witnessed rather than claiming to explain every part of the conflict.

Mensa discussed that same trip in a separate Everything Is Political interview, telling Celine Semaan that being in Palestine had shaped his perspective.

He said he drew on lived experience as well as reading, then used raps and essays to express his thoughts and observations.

He viewed Hip-Hop as a way to teach.

Asked specifically about the 2017 trip, he recalled watching a young Palestinian’s encounter with Israeli soldiers in Jerusalem while he was with Marc Lamont Hill.

The young man’s body language reminded him of Black youths dealing with police on Chicago’s South Side, Mensa said. In Hebron, he also recounted an encounter in which his American citizenship gave him freedom of movement that Palestinian companions did not have.

Mensa said an older man in a Bedouin camp had asked the visiting group to tell the outside world about what they had seen. He said he promised to do so.

In that interview, Mensa also called anti-Blackness a global problem, even as he credited his own religious practice with helping him treat people better.

He said his imam taught him not to judge others as though he were God.

El-Sayed recalled a Black teacher introducing him to civil-rights history after the September 11 attacks and argued against seeking acceptance at Black Americans’ expense.

item.title: 50 Cent Gets Thanked By Man Accused Of Attacking Rick Ross’ Son
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: 50 Cent shared an innocence claim and a personal thank-you on Instagram from the man accused of attacking Rick Ross' son.
item.content:encoded:
50 Cent got a public thank-you from the man accused of attacking Rick Ross’ son. His support for the accused had already drawn an angry response from the young man’s mother, Tia Kemp.

In the reel 50 shared on October 21, the man said:

“I appreciate everybody who believed in me, my family and my friends. I’m innocent. The Lord know I’m innocent. 50, I appreciate you for everything you’re doing for me and believing in my innocence.”

“I had a strong feeling this brother was innocent,” 50 wrote in the caption.

50 had previously offered to cover bond for the suspect. The man’s statement did not identify a payment or explain what help 50 had provided.

The dispute began with 50 mocking the news that Ross’ son had gone to police. His post suggested Ross might have made that call for him, but the police account identifies Ross’ son as the person who reported the incident.

Kemp, who shares William Roberts III with Ross, lashed out after 50 made that offer and asked for the suspect’s name, AllHipHop reported on October 21. “U have NO room to post anyone’s child,” she wrote. Her response then targeted his son Sire and Sire’s mother, Daphne Joy.

50 answered with a photo from a 2009 Smooth magazine shoot that featured him and Kemp together. Along with the image, he taunted Kemp and used the same response to promote his movie.

“Damn Tia you sound tougher than ya boy, I ain’t got time to argue with you,” he wrote.

Kemp also accused 50 of a double standard over bringing children into their dispute. She argued that he wanted boundaries for his own family while making other people’s children targets for his public attacks.

Her comments concerned 50’s earlier posts, not the man’s statement of innocence in the reel.

In its October 20 report on the case, AllHipHop said Ross’ son told police a man threatened him and struck him with a gun in Daytona Beach on October 11. The accused man was charged with aggravated assault and aggravated battery with a deadly weapon.

item.title: Shreveport Mayor Challenges 50 Cent To Deliver
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: 50 Cent's Shreveport criticism drew a response from Mayor Tom Arceneaux, who defended city support and sought a return call.
item.content:encoded:
Shreveport Mayor Tom Arceneaux challenged 50 Cent to deliver on his studio commitments, rejecting the rapper’s claim that City Hall had not backed him.

“Well, we have been most accommodating to Mr. Jackson from the very beginning, and now it’s time for him to perform,” Arceneaux told KSLA.

The mayor declined to comment on October 14, according to city communications director Leigh Anne Evensky.

Arceneaux said he wanted a return call and that no contract had been signed for the separate Red River District proposal. He said his call months earlier remained unanswered.

On “The Crew Has It,” 50 had questioned pouring more money into Shreveport without city support. He also said he still intended to do the work he had promised. He wanted recognition as a business owner and said earlier broken promises had made residents doubt new plans.

Red River is the city-owned entertainment area beneath the Texas Street Bridge. That proposal is separate from the larger studio plan. Inspections had found major repairs were needed there, and G-Unit wanted that work addressed before moving ahead.

The larger plan involved three sites, not just the riverfront entertainment area. Louisiana Economic Development’s January 12 announcement outlined more than $124 million in planned investment. Stageworks would be renovated for live events and production, Millennium Studios would be modernized, and a new dome-style immersive venue and park would be built downtown.

The state agreed to provide up to $50 million for eligible infrastructure and modernization work. That was performance-based support, tied to economic impact, local business involvement and delivery of the improvements.

An oversight body, the Shreveport Film & Entertainment Economic Development Corporation, was set up to work with the state agency on accountability for the project and its funds.

City Hall’s January 13 statement welcomed the state-backed plan while saying it required no additional municipal money. It put the estimated Millennium Studios investment at $78 million and Stageworks at $24 million, noting that both properties were leased to G-Unit.

There was already a separate Stageworks lease: the city and 50 signed it on June 6, 2025, for productions, events and multimedia work.

item.title: Warner Music Targets Film & TV Money With Licensing Shake-Up
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Warner Music Group moved to unite song-licensing teams, targeting film, TV, ad and game deals across its global catalog.
item.content:encoded:
Warner Music Group unveiled a plan to put one global boss in charge of its teams that license songs and recordings for films, TV shows, ads and games.

The company’s October 21 announcement promoted Ron Broitman to president of Global Sync. His team will span publisher Warner Chappell Music and label groups such as Atlantic Music Group and Warner Records Group.

Atlantic’s roster includes Cardi B, Missy Elliott and Jack Harlow.

Sync deals pair music with images. But a song and the recording of that song carry separate copyrights. A filmmaker who wants a specific recording generally needs permission for both the song and the master.

Warner said clients would have one place to seek licenses from its recording and publishing catalogs.

“We are making it easier and faster to license our entire global library,” Broitman said.

There is a growing pool of screen money at stake. The RIAA’s midyear report put U.S. recorded-music sync revenue at $231.8 million for the first half of 2026, up 18.2% from the same stretch last year. Those are industrywide wholesale receipts, not a tally of Warner’s earnings or artists’ take-home pay.

Warner Chappell CEO Guy Moot said the publisher’s team would remain part of the joint sync team to keep pitching its songwriters’ work.

item.title: Kurtis Blow & The D.O.C. Get Their Due At Paid In Full’s Vegas Gala
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Paid In Full Foundation will honor Kurtis Blow, The D.O.C., Nile Rodgers and Ralph McDaniels at its October 24 Las Vegas gala.
item.content:encoded:
The Paid In Full Foundation will put Kurtis Blow and The D.O.C. at the center of its next Hip Hop Grandmaster Awards, with a Las Vegas gala built around recognition and financial support for the people who helped create the culture.

The two MCs are the 2026 Grandmaster honorees for the October 24 event at the Bellagio. Nile Rodgers will receive the Quincy Jones Achievement Award, while Ralph McDaniels will receive the Contributor Award.

The foundation’s awards program pairs public honors with support for artists whose influence has not always brought matching financial rewards. The group says net proceeds from the gala will support that work, helping pioneers and other creatives pursue new projects.

Nas, Grandmaster Caz, Steve Stoute and Ben Horowitz discussed that mix of financial support and recognition in an a16z episode last month. Caz reflected on what the honor meant to his life and legacy.

This year’s honorees helped expand Hip-Hop in different ways. Kurtis Blow’s 1980 single “The Breaks” became the first gold-certified rap song. The D.O.C.’s platinum debut, “No One Can Do It Better,” arrived in 1989 through Ruthless Records, and his songwriting for N.W.A. and Dr. Dre extended his reach beyond his own records.

Rodgers’ connection runs through the music that early rappers built on. Chic’s “Good Times” provided the musical foundation for the Sugarhill Gang’s “Rapper’s Delight,” linking his work directly to rap’s early commercial breakthrough.

McDaniels helped give the culture a home on television. “Video Music Box” began in 1983, and New York City’s media office credited the host and producer with helping advance artists including LL Cool J and Jay-Z. In an AllHipHop interview last year, McDaniels also described the work of digitizing the show’s archive so those performances and interviews could reach new viewers.

The new group follows last year’s Bellagio honorees, including Kool G Rap, Grand Puba, Kool Rock Ski, Jalil Hutchins and George Clinton. Clinton’s recognition led to a memorable moment when he rapped “Follow The Leader” and Rakim joined him onstage.

The fourth annual gala is scheduled for Saturday, October 24, in the Bellagio’s Tower Ballroom.

Photo: Kurtis Blow im Musiktheater Bad (Hannover, Germany), 2012-03-30.JPG by Ferhat Ataman, via Wikimedia Commons. Cropped and resized; this image adaptation is licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0.

item.title: Sacha Baron Cohen Defends Ali G As Racism Debate Follows Movie Return
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Sacha Baron Cohen defended Ali G as a joke about white cultural theft, while critics questioned who really pays for the laugh.
item.content:encoded:
Sacha Baron Cohen defended Ali G against racism claims, arguing that the joke targeted a white man copying Black culture rather than the culture itself.

In a new TIME essay, Cohen called the character a fool whose borrowed style helps expose powerful people’s bias.

“The fact that Ali G is outdated and problematic is the very reason I resurrected him,” he wrote.

That defense speaks to a dispute that has followed Ali G for years: who is the audience really laughing at?

In 2000, comic Felix Dexter argued that Ali G let white middle-class viewers laugh at Black culture while still feeling free of racism.

NewsCord is a site that uses AI to compare news reports and flag bias. The site also helps readers send protest letters. Its Ali G campaign urges chains to refuse “Ali G: Who Iz I?” rather than sell tickets to what it views as racial mockery. The group has also asked Britain’s film ratings board how it judged the film’s racial jokes.

Its case goes back to Black British comics who spoke out years ago. It also cites complaints about Cohen’s other roles. It treats the new movie as part of that wider record, not a joke that can be judged only by what its creator says he meant.

Terry Gross put that same question to Cohen in 2007: did Borat’s jokes expose hatred of Jews or help it spread?

Cohen argued that Borat’s views were too wild to be taken as truth. The character thought Jews could turn into bugs. His aim, he told Gross, was to show how false such views were, not ask fans to share them.

His Jewish roots came up in their chat, too. “I’m proud to be a Jew,” Cohen said. He kept some customs out of that pride, though he said he was not religious.

But his concern went beyond people who held those views. When a bar crowd sang along with Borat’s anti-Jewish song, Cohen saw a danger in how easily they joined in. They did not have to hate Jews to help hate spread, he argued. They could simply go along with the song instead of speaking up or walking out.

For Cohen, Ali G’s joke lay in the gap between who he was and who he wanted to be. Cohen told Gross that Ali G saw himself as a Black Hip-Hop star from a tough part of town, though his home was a leafy suburb.

The dispute reached Druski’s team-up with Ali G earlier this month, which drew complaints about how the act used Black culture.

“Ali G: Who Iz I?” is due in U.K. theaters October 23.

Photo: DisclaimerBFILFF101024 (20 of 113) by Raph_PH, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0. Cropped and resized from original.
